Note that this will also be exposed to scripts in its current form. It shows up in the editor documentation as:
```
bool intersect_ray_struct(parameters: PhysicsRayQueryParameters3D, result: PhysicsServer3DExtensionRayResult*)
```
... which GDScript seems to treat as:
```
bool intersect_ray_struct(parameters: PhysicsRayQueryParameters3D, result: int)
```

I've always just assumed that this type of "return through a mutable reference/pointer parameter" is a no-go for bound methods for this reason. I can't recall having seen it anywhere else, except for `PhysicsDirectSpaceState3DExtension`, but that class isn't meant to be used from scripts to begin with. I guess if there's some way to restrict individual methods to only be exposed to GDExtension then this becomes less of a problem.

> and we'd probably want to expose a few more things with native structs too (perhaps `RayParameters`, `ShapeResult`, `ShapeParameters` and `ShapeRestInfo`?)

`RayParameters` and `ShapeParameters` are already exposed as `PhysicsRayQueryParameters3D` and `PhysicsShapeQueryParameters3D` respectively, and are passed as a pointer when used through GDExtension.

> I think the name still works because "Extension" could refer to it being usable via GDExtension.

By that logic the new method should probably be called `intersect_ray_extension` as well. `*_struct` seems like too much of a language-specific detail.

I would argue that "native" is probably a better term in this context, since the consuming language needs some ability to deal with pointers at least. "Extension" as it's used in the physics API currently is more about it being implemented by an extension, rather than being used from one.

> Note that this will also be exposed to scripts in its current form. It shows up in the editor documentation as:
> 
> ```
> bool intersect_ray_struct(parameters: PhysicsRayQueryParameters3D, result: PhysicsServer3DExtensionRayResult*)
> ```
> 
> ... which GDScript seems to treat as:
> 
> ```
> bool intersect_ray_struct(parameters: PhysicsRayQueryParameters3D, result: int)
> ```

Yeah, this is the case for all methods that use `GDExtensionPtr<T>`

On the one hand, it would be kind of nice to have a flag for methods to prevent exposing them to scripting - this has come up a bunch of times before in other situations.

But on the other hand, I think it _should_ theoretically be possible for a scripting language to allow access to native structs depending on the language's features. Like, GDScript can't do it, but I could imagine a way for C# to do it (even through the scripting API), or other scripting languages added via GDExtension like Python.

I wonder if maybe GDScript should filter these methods out, because it specifically can't handle them?

Although, it still wouldn't be the most convenient to work with structs in a scripting language, so maybe that's a reason to exclude them entirely.

> I've always just assumed that this type of "return through a mutable reference/pointer parameter" is a no-go for bound methods for this reason. I can't recall having seen it anywhere else, except for `PhysicsDirectSpaceState3DExtension`, but that class isn't meant to be used from scripts to begin with.

We don't do it very often, but there are a couple instances of it. For example, with `AudioFrame` in places like `AudioEffectInstance::_process()`

> `RayParameters` and `ShapeParameters` are already exposed as `PhysicsRayQueryParameters3D` and `PhysicsShapeQueryParameters3D` respectively, and are passed as a pointer when used through GDExtension.

Yeah, my thinking was that since those just wrap structs, it could make sense for the struct version of the method to take them directly too. But maybe for consistency with the non-struct versions, it'd be best to keep those wrapper objects? Also, it's nice that with the wrapper object you don't need to clear fields that you don't use, so that's another argument for keeping those

> By that logic the new method should probably be called `intersect_ray_extension` as well. `*_struct` seems like too much of a language-specific detail.

That makes sense! I'll update it to that

> On the one hand, it would be kind of nice to have a flag for methods to prevent exposing them to scripting - this has come up a bunch of times before in other situations.
> 
> But on the other hand, I think it _should_ be possible for a scripting language to allow access to native structs depending on the language's features. Like, GDScript can't do it, but I could imagine a way for C# to do it (even through the scripting API), or other scripting languages added via GDExtension like Python.

Given that GDScript is likely used by the majority of projects out there, I would maybe go so far as to say that it should be a prerequisite for this flag to exist, or for GDScript to somehow be able to deal with these types of arguments. It seems unfortunate to otherwise end up having two `intersect_ray*` methods show up in the auto-completion with one of them being unusable.

> We don't do it very often, but there are a couple instances of it. For example, with `AudioFrame` in places like `AudioEffectInstance::_process()`

`AudioEffectInstance::_process` doesn't seem to be callable from GDScript though, as far as I can tell, maybe because of the leading underscore?

> Yeah, my thinking was that since those just wrap structs, it could make sense for the struct version of the method to take them directly too. But maybe for consistency with the non-struct versions, it'd be best to keep those wrapper objects?

I guess one argument for *not* relying on the wrapper classes are languages like C# (i.e. when hosting libgodot or whatever) where declaring a type as `class` versus `struct` to some degree dictates whether it will be allocated on the heap or the stack. But that also assumes that all our `GDREGISTER_NATIVE_STRUCT` declarations are compatible with whatever limitations the language might have on their structs. I know C# has (or at least had) a bunch for their `ref struct` types, i.e. structs that are guaranteed to be stack-allocated.

I think I'd rather see this problem (functions returning dictionaries when we'd rather have typed low-cost objects) solved with [structs](https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/7329) or [custom variants](https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/11797).

I'd be unhappy with a solution that would be different for GDExtensions and GDScript. We'd be solving the problem only for some of the people.

@raulsntos I implemented your suggestion almost exactly (as `intersect_ray_no_alloc` and `PhysicsRayQueryResult3D` for clarity) and have some very good looking preliminary benchmarks to show for it. If it's okay with you, I'll open a PR after I clean it up to meet conventions/standards and do some more testing. For a pretty good representitive workload (see below), this gives ~35% speedup in gdscript, and ~267% speedup in C++ versus the regular dictionary returning method, and should work in all languages and be backwards compatible (didn't modify any methods). NOTE: The percentages above are for GodotPhysics3D since I was testing on 4.5.1 and it's the default, I'll test Jolt as well when I begin testing in later versions of the engine. I wonder if the difference will be similar :) To understand the numbers below (until I put together some visualizations and a more isolated benchmark), each cell is the average number of microseconds taken to execute the `update_simulation` method on a PBD rope solver, scaled by number of particles for the columns named `p_count_*`. For the rows, fast raycast means only one raycast per particle per call to `update_simulation`, and accurate raycast means n raycasts per particle per call to `update_simulation`, where n is the number of solver iterations (in this case 4). The averages were obtained by benching each cell 1000 times, with warmup iterations.
